newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No Euro-Parliament decision next week on Tapie.
newsitem.headline: No Euro-Parliament decision next week on Tapie.

text.p: The European Parliament -- in limbo until its presidential elections are held on Tuesday -- will not take any decision next week on whether to throw out bankrupt French businessan Bernard Tapie, officials said on Friday.

Parliamentary officials were reacting to a decision by France's top administrative court on Wednesday to reject an appeal by embattled Tapie to retain his seat in the parliament, his last political job.

The Council of State turned down Tapie's request to suspend a French government decree removing him from the Strasbourg parliament after a court declared him ineligible for public office as a bankrupt.

For the European Parliament to act, its president must be formally notified of the French decision and that will be impracticable before Tuesday's election in Strasbourg of the new president, officials explained.
The parliament committee which will have to prepare the decision will not be able to meet until its new chairman is elected on Thursday next week, the official said.
The parliament's president, vice presidents and other officers are elected half way through the assembly's five year term.
The official said a decision would be taken when deputies meet for two days in Brussels on January 29-30 or at the latest when the parliament next meets in Strasbourg.

The Council of State ruling, released to the press, appeared to spell the end of the political road for Tapie, a flamboyant ex-cabinet minister who has already been stripped of his seat in the French National Assembly.

It had deferred a decision to strip him of his seat after his lawyers argued that Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decree, issued last November, was unprecedented in the history of the assembly and created a situation not provided for in its rules.

Tapie, the target of a blizzard of legal actions over his now collapsed business empire and the Marseille soccer team he once ran, has been sentenced to jail terms of eight and six months for tax fraud and rigging a soccer match.

He is appealing in both cases to the French supreme court and has promised to resign from the European Parliament if the court confirms his sentence for match-rigging at the Olympique Marseille. The ruling is expected on February 4.
